cards.back: A study in which two groups are compared under identical conditions except for one variable (the treatment). One group receives the treatment; the other (control group) does not.
The group in an experiment that receives no treatment or a placebo. It serves as a baseline for comparison to see if the treatment had an effect.
The group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.
Randomly assigning subjects to the treatment group or control group. This minimizes bias and makes the groups similar in all ways before the treatment is applied.
cards.front: What does [[kw:randomization]] mean in an experiment?

cards.back: A controlled experiment where subjects are randomly assigned to the control group or the treatment group. This design can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
A harmless, fake treatment (like a sugar pill) that looks like the real treatment. It is given to the control group to prevent psychological effects from influencing results.

cards.front: How does an experiment differ from an observational study?
cards.back: In an experiment, a treatment is imposed and subjects are randomly assigned to groups (can show causation). In an observational study, subjects are observed without imposing a treatment (can only show correlation).

Because the groups may differ in ways other than the variable being studied. [[imp:Confounding variables]] can affect the results, so we can only say there is an association, not that one variable causes the other.
cards.front: Why can observational studies not prove causation?

cards.back: A variable other than the treatment that could affect the results of an experiment. It makes it hard to determine the true cause of an effect.
Repeating an experiment under the same or similar conditions. It confirms that results are not just a one-time fluke and increases reliability.

cards.front: Why is a large [[kw:sample size]] important in an experiment?
cards.back: Larger samples reduce the effect of chance and make the results more reliable. Small samples can be skewed by a few unusual individuals.

An experimental design where subjects are first grouped by a similar characteristic (like age or gender), and then within each block, randomly assigned to treatment or control. This controls for the effect of that characteristic.

cards.front: Identify the flaw: 'Patients chose whether to take vitamin C; after a year, the vitamin C group had 15% lower cholesterol.'
cards.back: Not a randomized comparative experiment — patients chose their own group. This is an observational study with self-selection. The conclusion may not be valid because healthier patients might have chosen to take the supplement.
Gender is completely confounded with the treatment. We don't know if the difference is due to the gum or to gender. The design should randomly assign gum/placebo within each gender group.
cards.front: Identify the flaw: '10,000 overweight people: females get the new weight‑loss gum, males get a placebo. Females lose more weight.'

cards.back: A phenomenon where people experience a real improvement simply because they believe they are receiving a treatment, even if it's a placebo. A control group with a placebo accounts for this effect.
